deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the R.PFunctionen bundle, Riemann's notes on the P-function and hypergeometric functions. The next page treats the logarithmic case: δ = α − γ − 1, derivatives with respect to α and δ, and a log x · Σ term. On the present page Riemann comments on a set of relations he has just derived, which are probably connection formulas between Euler-type integral representations. He then shows how to free them from a convergence restriction.

(1) Text, roughly: 'All these relations hold at first only under the assumption that α, β, γ, δ are real and > −1.' He then extends them to complex values: they hold for imaginary values whenever the real parts are > −1, since the integrals and their derivatives with respect to α, β, γ stay finite there. This is the usual argument by analyticity and continuity in the parameters. He then announces a way to remove the restriction ('In diesem Umfange…'): replace the part of the integral up to the endpoints by loop integrals.

(2) The integral (my reading) is P(α,β,γ,x) ~ ∫_0^1 s^α (1−s)^β (1−xs)^γ ds. This converges only for Re α > −1 and Re β > −1. Riemann splits it as
∫_0^1 = ∫_ε^{1−ε'} + ∫_0^ε + ∫_{1−ε'}^1.

(3) Key identity, written as ∫_0^ε = 1/(e^{2απi} − 1) · ∫_{εe^{0i}}^{εe^{2πi}}.
- The right-hand integral runs over the small circle |s| = ε, starting at arg s = 0 and ending at arg s = 2π, with s^α followed continuously.
- Proof (filled in by me): the integrand is s^α·f(s) with f holomorphic near 0. Shrink the circle to a path along [0, ε] traversed twice. Going out with arg 0 gives −∫_0^ε s^α f ds. Coming back with arg 2π gives e^{2πiα} ∫_0^ε s^α f ds.
- So the loop integral equals (e^{2πiα} − 1) ∫_0^ε s^α f ds, which is valid for Re α > −1.
- The left side then gets an expression whose right-hand side is holomorphic in α except at integers. This gives the analytic continuation to Re α ≤ −1.

(4) The same is done at s = 1 with the factor 1/(e^{2βπi} − 1), integrating around s = 1 starting and ending at 1 − ε'. The resulting regularized integral is
∫_ε^{1−ε'} + 1/(e^{2απi}−1) ∮_ε + (±) 1/(e^{2βπi}−1) ∮_{1−ε'}.
It is independent of ε and ε', and it defines P for all non-integral α, β. A '+' before the β-term is struck out and the sign is hard to read.

(5) Bottom: 'log x Σ' is a memo for the next page. When exponents become integers the factors 1/(e^{2απi}−1) have poles. Taking limits then means differentiating with respect to α, which produces log x times a series. This is the logarithmic (degenerate) case treated overleaf.
errors: The orientation and sign of the loop term at s = 1 are ambiguous. With (1−s)^β continued counterclockwise around s = 1 from 1−ε', the loop integral equals (1 − e^{2πiβ}) ∫_{1−ε'}^1. So the term needs the factor −1/(e^{2βπi} − 1) for a counterclockwise loop, or +1/(e^{2βπi} − 1) for a clockwise loop. The page's '+' (after a struck-out '+') is correct only under the clockwise convention, which is not stated.
The extension argument 'integrals and their derivatives remain finite' implicitly relies on uniform convergence and analyticity in the parameters. This is fine but unstated.
The formula fails at integer α (respectively β), where e^{2απi} − 1 = 0. That case is deferred to the logarithmic treatment on the next page.

results.what: Analytic continuation in the exponent of an Euler/beta-type integral ∫ s^α(1−s)^β(1−xs)^γ ds by replacing the endpoint pieces with small loop integrals divided by (e^{2πiα} − 1). This is a regularization of divergent endpoint integrals.
results.modern_name: Loop (Hankel-type) contour regularization of Euler integrals; precursor of the Pochhammer double-loop contour / regularized beta integral
results.usually_credited_to: Hankel (1864, Gamma function loop); Pochhammer (1890, double loop for hypergeometric integrals); Jordan and others for the regularization

results.what: Extending relations proven for real exponents > −1 to complex exponents with real part > −1, via finiteness and analyticity of the integrals in the parameters.
results.modern_name: Analytic continuation / identity theorem in the parameters

results.what: Note 'log x Σ': at integer exponent differences the connection formulas acquire log x times a power series, obtained by differentiating with respect to the exponent.
results.modern_name: Logarithmic solutions of the hypergeometric equation (Frobenius-type degenerate case)

deep.surprise_reason: Riemann already used a Hankel-type loop contour around a branch point in his 1859 zeta paper, before Hankel 1864. His hypergeometric lecture notes (published in the Nachträge) work with such integrals. A loop-integral regularization of the endpoint singularities of the Euler integral is therefore a natural, mildly notable unpublished detail, not a new attribution. It foreshadows Pochhammer, but the double-loop idea itself does not appear here.

checkable.asserts: For f = 1: the loop integral over |s| = ε from arg 0 to 2π, divided by (e^{2πiα} − 1), equals ∫_0^ε s^α ds = ε^{α+1}/(α+1). Expected result 0 for non-integer α.
The regularized ∫_0^1 s^α ds via the loop formula gives 1/(α+1) also for α = −3/2, where the ordinary integral diverges (the analytic continuation). Expected result 0.

Endpoint s = 1 with u = 1 − s: going counterclockwise around s = 1 corresponds, after reversing orientation, to the sign factor (1 − e^{2πiβ}). This fixes the sign of the β-term (up to orientation). Expected result 0 (the orientation reversal is accounted for in the stated factor).

transcription_corrections: Line 2 likely reads 'gelten zunächst nur unter der Voraussetzung, daß α, β, γ, δ reell und größer als −1 sind'.
Line 4–5: probably 'Hieraus folgt sie für imaginäre Werthe, wenn der reelle Theil > −1, … Da die Integrale und ihre Differentialquotienten nach α, β, γ endlich bleiben'. The 'noch' is likely 'nach'.
'In diesem Umfange kann man …' is likely 'Um diese Einschränkung zu heben, kann man … das Integral bis zu ε ersetzen durch …' (uncertain).
The second term's limits are εe^{0i} to εe^{2πi} (loop around 0), not ∫_ε^ε. The third term is a loop starting and ending at 1−ε'.
